mcqs.question: Which of the following statements correctly compares the lenses used to correct myopia with those used to correct hypermetropia?

options.A: Myopia is corrected with convex lenses, which converge light before it reaches the eye
options.B: Myopia is corrected with concave lenses, which diverge light so that the focal point moves backward
options.C: Both myopia and hypermetropia are corrected with convex lenses
options.D: Both myopia and hypermetropia are corrected with concave lenses

mcqs.answer: Myopia is corrected with concave lenses, which diverge light so that the focal point moves backward
mcqs.explanation: Myopia (near‑sightedness) is corrected by placing a diverging (concave) lens in front of the eye; this lens spreads the incoming rays so that the image is formed on the retina. Hypermetropia (far‑sightedness) requires a converging (convex) lens to bring the focal point forward onto the retina. Therefore option B accurately describes the comparison, while the other options misstate the type of lens needed for each defect.

mcqs.question: How is hypermetropia defined in the context of refractive errors of the eye?

options.A: A condition in which the image of a distant object is formed behind the retina, requiring additional converging power to focus on the retina
options.B: A condition in which the image of a distant object is formed in front of the retina, requiring diverging lenses to correct
options.C: A condition where the image is formed exactly on the retina without any correction
options.D: A condition caused by the cornea being too steep, leading to image formation at the corneal surface

mcqs.answer: A condition in which the image of a distant object is formed behind the retina, requiring additional converging power to focus on the retina
mcqs.explanation: In hypermetropia (far‑sightedness) the eye is too short or the cornea too flat, so parallel rays from a distant object converge behind the retina. A convex (converging) lens adds the needed power to bring the focal point onto the retina. Option A states this correctly; the other options describe opposite or unrelated situations.

mcqs.question: What is the primary anatomical cause of hypermetropia?

options.A: The eyeball is shorter than normal or the cornea is flatter, causing the focal point to lie behind the retina
options.B: The eyeball is longer than normal, causing the focal point to lie in front of the retina
options.C: The lens becomes too thick, moving the focal point forward onto the retina
options.D: The retina is positioned too far forward within the eye

mcqs.answer: The eyeball is shorter than normal or the cornea is flatter, causing the focal point to lie behind the retina
mcqs.explanation: Hypermetropia results when the axial length of the eye is reduced or the corneal curvature is insufficient, so parallel rays focus beyond the retina. Option A captures this cause. Option B describes myopia, while C and D are not causes of hypermetropia.

mcqs.question: Which type of lens should be prescribed to correct hypermetropia?
mcqs.explanation: Hypermetropia requires additional converging power to move the focal point forward onto the retina; a convex lens provides this. Concave lenses are used for myopia, plano lenses have no power, and cylindrical lenses correct astigmatism, not hypermetropia.

mcqs.question: Which definition best describes myopia?

options.A: A condition where distant objects are seen clearly but near objects are blurred because the image forms in front of the retina
options.B: A condition where near objects are seen clearly but distant objects are blurred because the image forms behind the retina
options.C: A condition where images are formed on the retina but are distorted due to irregular corneal shape
options.D: A condition caused by loss of lens elasticity, affecting near vision in older adults

mcqs.answer: A condition where distant objects are seen clearly but near objects are blurred because the image forms in front of the retina
mcqs.explanation: Myopia (near‑sightedness) occurs when the eye is too long or the cornea too curved, causing parallel rays to converge before reaching the retina. Thus distant objects are clear, near objects are not. Option A states this correctly; the other options describe hypermetropia, astigmatism, and presbyopia respectively.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is the main cause of myopia?
mcqs.explanation: Myopia arises when the axial length of the eye increases (or the cornea becomes too steep), so the focal point falls in front of the retina. Option B correctly identifies this cause. Shortening the eye leads to hypermetropia, flattening the cornea reduces focusing power, and lens weakening is associated with presbyopia.

mcqs.question: A student has myopia and requires a corrective lens of –2.5 dioptres. Which lens will correct his vision?
mcqs.explanation: Myopia is corrected with a diverging (concave) lens whose power is negative. A –2.5 D concave lens will shift the focal point backward onto the retina. Positive (convex) lenses would worsen myopia, and a concave lens cannot have positive power.

mcqs.question: Riya can see distant road signs clearly but finds it difficult to read a book held at 30 cm. Which refractive error does she most likely have?
mcqs.explanation: Riya’s difficulty with near objects while distant vision is clear indicates far‑sightedness (hypermetropia). Myopia would cause trouble with distant vision, astigmatism produces blurred vision at all distances, and presbyopia occurs in older adults due to loss of lens flexibility.
